newsitem.title: UK: Europe fuel tanker rates rise for Russian summer.
newsitem.headline: Europe fuel tanker rates rise for Russian summer.

text.p: Northwest European fuel oil tanker chartering rates for 25,000 tonne vessels have risen by nearly two dollars a tonne in recent days and brokers say this is likely to continue as the seasonal flood of Russian exports gathers pace.
London shipbrokers said fresh fixtures on Wednesday of 25,000 tonners - the main work horses for carrying heavy fuel oil within northwest Europe - were being seen at Worldscale rates as high as W220.
That is equivalent to roughly $8.50 a tonne for a typical voyage, compared to average rates a month ago of around W185, or $7 a tonne.
"There is precious little tonnage available within May dates and anyone who needs an early cargo is going to have to pay up," one broker said. "We have seen a steady increase in the last two weeks."
"We saw rates up to W270 in summer last year and W300 in 1995 and this year seems to be following a similar pattern."
Russian exports traditionally boom during the summer months as local demand declines and iced-up winter export routes thaw.

One of these key arteries - the Volga river system connecting inland refineries to key Baltic export terminals at St.Petersburg - became navigable recently as the temperature rose and traders have seen exports gather steam.

Industry consultants Petro Logistics said in a weekly report that exports from the Baltics and the Black Sea in the first week of May amounted to around 330,000 barrels per day (bpd) compared to around 170,000 bpd in the first week of January.
Brokers said rates last year rose from January's numbers as low as W165 up to W270 in June, then fell again in August back down to around W185.
A similar pattern emerged last year.
One dealer said that even though there was plenty of available tonnage in early June he expected it to be snapped up quickly.
"I cannot imagine rates are going to drop from here."
He added that higher rates were unlikely to attract a large number of extra vessels from other regions.

"It is something of a closed shop up here," he said. "You tend to see the same ships trading the region although some of the clean tankers may find it profitable to convert to taking fuel if the premium is good enough."
He said that rates for 50,000 tonners in Europe were harder to assess because they tended to ply a variety of different routes.
